headline: The world now has more seniors than young children

sources.title: Global Older Adult Population Projected to Nearly Double by 2060 (U.S. Census Bureau)
Historic first: Older adults now outnumber the youngest children worldwide (Axios)
Worldwide Population Hits 'Tipping Point' Earlier Than Expected (Newsweek)

chunks.text: The world now has more people aged 65 and older than children aged 5 and younger, the U.S. Census Bureau said in a report that {{came out}} on August 31, 2026. Between 2020 and 2025, the [[share]] of older adults {{caught up with}} and passed the youngest children's share for the first time in [[recorded history]]. The report, by Census Bureau [[demographers]], {{pulls together}} population [[figures]] from every country.

verbs.wrong: To be counted in a survey
verbs.why: A new album comes out every spring, and the exam results come out in July. The Census Bureau's report on aging came out on August 31, 2026.

verbs.correct: To reach the same level as
verbs.wrong: To be measured at the same time
verbs.why: A runner can catch up with the leader on the last lap, and a small company can catch up with a bigger rival. Between 2020 and 2025, the share of older adults caught up with the share of the youngest children and then passed it.
A coach pulls together a team from three schools, and a reporter pulls together facts from many interviews. The report pulls together population figures from every country in the world.

chunks.text: Two things {{lie behind}} the change: people are living longer, and [[birth rates]] have {{gone down}}. In 2023, 71 percent of people lived in countries where women have 2.1 children or fewer [[on average]], the number needed to {{keep up}} a population. In 2013 it was 45 percent. China, India and Mexico are among them. The [[shift]] is {{speeding up}}: the world passed this "[[tipping point]]" much earlier than experts expected a [[decade]] ago, the report says.

verbs.correct: To be the cause of something
verbs.wrong: To be expected in the future
verbs.why: Money worries often lie behind a family argument, and a small mistake can lie behind a big accident. Two things lie behind the world's aging: longer lives and lower birth rates.
Gas prices go down in the winter, and a fever goes down after a day in bed. Birth rates have gone down in most of the world, so there are fewer young children.

verbs.correct: To hold at the same level
verbs.why: A shop has to keep up its stock in the busy season, and a runner tries to keep up her speed on the hills. Women need to have about 2.1 children on average to keep up a country's population.

Traffic speeds up once you leave the city, and a computer speeds up after you delete old files. The shift toward an older world is speeding up, and it passed this tipping point much earlier than experts expected.

chunks.text: Japan is the oldest country, with 29.7 percent of its people aged 65 or older, but South Korea is expected to {{take over}} the [[top spot]] by 2060, at 41 percent. Europe is the oldest [[region]], yet Africa's older population is expected to {{shoot up}} by more than 300 percent, to 249 million by 2060, against 214 million in Europe. The United States, 48th oldest in 2025, is expected to {{end up}} 110th by 2060 as other countries age faster.

verbs.correct: To replace another at the top
verbs.wrong: To look like an older relative
verbs.why: A new champion takes over from the old one, and a younger manager can take over from her boss. South Korea is expected to take over the top spot from Japan as the world's oldest country by 2060.

verbs.wrong: To try to reach a goal
verbs.why: Rents shoot up when a new factory opens, and a child's height can shoot up in a single summer. Africa's older population is expected to shoot up by more than 300 percent by 2060.
A late bus can end up an hour behind schedule, and a weak team can end up last in the league. The United States is expected to end up 110th on the list of oldest countries by 2060.

chunks.text: The report {{points out}} that 73 percent of older Americans had two or more [[chronic conditions]] between 2016 and 2019. One expert who [[contributed]] to the report said old age could {{turn into}} an economic [[asset]] if countries [[invest]] in [[preventive health]] and let people {{stay on}} at work longer. By 2060 the world's older population is expected to reach nearly 2 billion, up from 852 million in 2025, and {{make up}} one in five people worldwide.

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.wrong: To be a sign of something
verbs.why: A coach points out that the team always plays better after a long rest, and a neighbor points out that the trash is collected a day late this week. The report points out that 73 percent of older Americans had two or more chronic conditions between 2016 and 2019.

verbs.wrong: To refuse an offer or plan
verbs.why: A light rain can turn into a storm, and a small shop can turn into a big chain. One contributor says old age could turn into an economic asset rather than a cost.

verbs.correct: To keep a job longer than usual
verbs.wrong: To remain at home all day
verbs.why: A teacher may stay on for a year after retirement age, and a coach can stay on after the season ends. The report suggests letting older people stay on at work longer.

verbs.correct: To form a part of a total
verbs.why: Women make up half of the workforce, and students make up most of the town's population. By 2060, people aged 65 and older are expected to make up about one in five people on Earth.

mainIdea.s: A Census Bureau report says people aged 65 and older now outnumber children aged 5 and younger worldwide. Low birth rates and longer lives drive the change, and the group may reach 2 billion by 2060.
mainIdea.why: Between 2020 and 2025 the share of older adults passed the share of the youngest children for the first time, and the group is expected to grow from 852 million to nearly 2 billion by 2060.

mainIdea.s: For the first time, the world's older adults outnumber its youngest children. The report says the change arrived later than experts expected because birth rates fell more slowly than predicted.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the report says the world passed this tipping point much earlier than experts expected a decade ago, and the shift is speeding up, not slowing.

mainIdea.s: The United States has become one of the world's oldest countries, with nearly one in four residents over 65. Officials warn that pension and hospital costs will rise sharply over the next decade.
mainIdea.why: The United States was only the 48th oldest country in 2025 and is expected to end up 110th by 2060. The main finding is about the whole world's older adults passing its youngest children.

lines.text: Did you see the Census Bureau report that {{came out}} last week? The world now has more people aged 65 and older than kids aged 5 and younger.
More seniors than toddlers? [[History in the making]].
Literally. The share of older adults {{caught up with}} the youngest children between 2020 and 2025, for the first time in recorded history.
Two things {{lie behind}} it. People live longer, and birth rates have {{gone down}} almost everywhere. Seventy-one percent of people now live in countries where women have 2.1 children or fewer.
And 2.1 is the number you need to {{keep up}} a population, right?
Right. Ten years earlier it was 45 percent. The whole thing is {{speeding up}}.
Japan right now, at almost 30 percent. But South Korea is expected to {{take over}} by 2060, at 41 percent.
And Africa's older population is going to {{shoot up}} by more than 300 percent. By 2060, Africa will have more seniors than Europe.
It's 48th oldest today and will {{end up}} 110th, because everyone else is aging faster. [[Do the math]]: nearly 2 billion seniors by 2060, one in five of us.
That's a lot of pensions and hospital beds.

Well, the report {{points out}} that most older Americans already have two or more chronic conditions. But one contributor says old age could {{turn into}} an economic asset if people stay healthy and {{stay on}} at work longer.
[[It cuts both ways]], then. Longer lives, but only if they're healthy ones.
Exactly. Invest in preventive health and keep people working. [[That's a tall order]].
